analysis.one_liner: Imposes performance, error-remedy, and multilingual-service requirements on federal student loan servicers' contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on June 7, 2024, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Education Department to vet federal student loan servicers on past performance, consumer complaints, penalties, and legal actions before signing contracts. It would require contracts to include borrower protections: no interest accrues during servicer errors, borrowers get credit toward loan forgiveness for time lost to those errors, overpayments and fees caused by servicer mistakes are refunded, and erroneous negative marks are removed from credit reports. It also requires multilingual and disability-accessible borrower forms, allows contract revocation for servicer misrepresentation, and orders a government study of how loan transfers harm borrowers' credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers, especially those harmed by servicer errors: they would get interest-free forbearance while errors are fixed, forgiveness credit for time lost to errors, refunds of overpayments and fees, and removal of wrongly reported delinquencies. Borrowers with limited English proficiency and disabilities would get accessible forms and services.

how_it_helps.text: Servicers would have to place loans into administrative forbearance with no interest accruing during any period a servicer error remains uncorrected, and time in that forbearance would count as a qualifying payment toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness [S2].
Servicers would have to refund overpayments and reimburse fees caused by their errors, and ensure credit bureaus remove delinquencies that resulted from servicer mistakes [S2].

Before signing a servicing contract, the Education Department would have to evaluate a servicer's past performance, consumer satisfaction, penalties imposed by the Department, and legal actions taken against it, including by states [S2].
Borrower rights information would have to be available in multiple languages, including Spanish, Mandarin, Haitian Creole, and Arabic, and accessible to borrowers with disabilities [S2].

The Department could revoke a servicer contract if the servicer knowingly withheld information or misrepresented itself during vetting, and would have to review all legacy servicing contracts against the new standards [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal student loan servicers, which would bear compliance costs, mandatory borrower remedies, and the risk of contract revocation for misrepresentation. Because servicers are paid through Department of Education contracts, some compliance costs would ultimately flow to taxpayers through contract prices.

drawbacks.text: Stricter vetting and mandatory error remedies would raise servicers' operating costs, and since servicers are paid under federal contracts, taxpayers could pay more for servicing [S2].

The new contract terms apply only to contracts entered into 90 days after enactment, with existing legacy contracts merely reviewed rather than immediately converted, so protections for current borrowers would arrive slowly [S2].
Past-performance vetting relies on Department metrics and the Secretary's discretion, which supporters of servicers would argue could be applied inconsistently or favor incumbents [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the direct benefits are concrete: errors that currently cost them money, credit damage, and lost forgiveness credit would carry mandatory fixes at the servicer's expense. The main cost is higher servicing contract prices passed to taxpayers, and the slowest protections go to borrowers under existing legacy contracts. On balance the bill shifts error costs from borrowers to the companies that make the errors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sara Jacobs introduced the Student Loan Servicers Accountability Act of 2024 in the House on June 7, 2024 [S1].
The bill's only action after introduction was a referral to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, where it received no further action [S4].
The bill attracted 24 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no Republican support [S3].
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without ever reaching a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal student loan servicers are better off: they keep their Education Department contracts without the new vetting standards, mandatory error remedies, or revocation risk the bill would have imposed. Borrowers harmed by servicer errors gain nothing.

for.name: Rep. Sara Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action; the bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 supporters — the sponsor and 24 cosponsors — were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led committee never acted on the bill [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would bind servicers to mandatory borrower remedies, interest-free forbearance during their own errors, enhanced vetting, and possible contract revocation for misrepresentation. Their gain from the bill dying is continued freedom from those contract terms.
Servicers would be required to have credit bureaus remove delinquencies and other negative information caused by servicer errors, reducing negative-data volume and disputes that generate fees.
